title: Social Media Marketing for Luxury Real Estate in Bangalore
description: Social media planning for luxury developers and premium housing projects in Bangalore: walkthrough content, launch phases, NRI buyers and lead handling.
h1: Social Media Marketing for Luxury Real Estate in Bangalore
intro: A luxury home is rarely bought on a single visit, and almost never by a single person. A buyer may follow a project for months, share it with a spouse and parents, send it to a relative abroad and ask an adviser before booking a site visit. Social media is where much of that slow persuasion now happens. Our plans for premium developers treat it as a way to qualify and nurture serious buyers, not as a place to post renders and hope.

sections.h2: How luxury home buyers research and decide
paragraphs: The buyer is usually a household. One person finds the project, another checks the builder's record, and a third wants to know about schools, commute and resale. That is why a single hero image on a profile does very little. Buyers look for evidence across the profile: how consistently the developer posts, whether construction updates are honest, whether the location is explained plainly and whether the team answers questions in the comments.

A significant group of buyers are returning or overseas residents who cannot visit easily. They rely on video, clear process explanations and quick responses on messaging apps. If your social presence cannot answer their first ten questions, they will move on to a competitor who can.

sections.h2: Content that earns a site visit
paragraphs: We plan content around the questions a considered buyer actually asks, grouped into a few durable pillars.
bullets: Project walkthroughs shot properly, with a continuous route through the home and the shared spaces, not a montage of renders.
Location stories that explain the neighbourhood in practical terms: access, daily needs, schools, green space, noise and how the area feels at different hours.
Construction progress updates that show real stages on a regular schedule, which build more credibility than any slogan.
Design and material detail: what goes into a kitchen, a façade, a lobby, and why those choices were made.
Buying process explainers for first-time and overseas buyers, kept general and pointing to qualified advisers for anything legal or financial.
The team and the track record: who is building the project and what they have delivered before, stated factually.

paragraphs: A project passes through distinct phases and the social plan should change with them. Before launch, the aim is to build a list of interested buyers and let them see the thinking behind the project. At launch, content shifts to clarity: what is available, how to visit and what happens after an enquiry. During construction, the emphasis moves to progress and reassurance. After completion, the content turns to community, handover and referrals.

We map these phases for each project separately. A developer with several projects in different parts of the city should not run a single blended feed, because buyers of a Sarjapur Road family home and a central luxury apartment are not the same audience.

Instagram carries the visual impression and works well for short tours and construction moments. YouTube is the home of the full walkthrough and the location explainer, and those videos keep earning views long after they are posted. Meta lead campaigns can reach defined audiences, and we design the lead forms with qualifying questions so the sales team receives fewer, better enquiries. WhatsApp closes the gap between interest and a visit by letting the team answer privately and quickly.

We avoid channels where the audience does not match. LinkedIn becomes relevant for commercial leasing or for reaching overseas professionals, but for most luxury residential projects it is a minor part of the plan.

The numbers that matter are site-visit bookings, the proportion of enquiries that fit the project's buyer profile, and how many buyers who watched a walkthrough later made an enquiry. We also review the questions that sales staff hear most often, because they reveal where the content is not yet answering a worry.

We do not count renders liked or followers gained as success. A project with a modest audience that produces a steady flow of well-qualified visits is outperforming a project with a large audience and an empty sales room.

sections.h2: Rules to check before anything is published
paragraphs: Real estate advertising in India is regulated, including the display of project registration details under RERA. Claims about possession timelines, amenities and approvals must match what the project actually has. Renders and sample flats should be labelled for what they are. We recommend that your legal adviser reviews advertising templates and that you check current rules for every campaign, because requirements and enforcement change. [VERIFY WITH CLIENT COUNSEL]

sections.h2: Mistakes we see in property social media
paragraphs: Most developer feeds fail for predictable reasons, and fixing them is often the quickest win.
bullets: Posting only renders, which buyers have learned to discount, and never showing real progress on site.
Running the same creative for every project, so that an entry-level apartment and a premium villa sound identical.
Sending every enquiry straight to a sales team without a first qualifying question, which wastes the team's time and frustrates buyers.
Ignoring comments that ask about location or approvals, which signals that nobody is listening.
Treating the launch day as the whole campaign, then going silent for months while buyers are still deciding.

sections.h2: What the first ninety days look like
paragraphs: In the first month we audit your profiles, your enquiry process and your competitors, and agree the buyer profile for each project. In the second month we produce the first walkthrough and location content and start a regular progress-update rhythm. In the third month we review which content produced visits, adjust the lead questions and decide whether paid campaigns deserve a place. By the end of the quarter you should know, from your own sales data, which buyers are responding.

sections.h2: What a custom plan includes for a developer
paragraphs: The scope depends on how many projects you run, which phases they are in, how much video you can support and whether paid campaigns are part of the plan. Typical elements are a content strategy per project, a production schedule for walkthrough and progress video, campaign and lead-form design, an enquiry-handling process with your sales team, and monthly reporting tied to site visits. You receive the exact scope in writing after the free audit.

faqs.q: Can you plan a pre-launch campaign for a project that has not been announced?
faqs.a: Yes. Pre-launch work focuses on building an interested audience through design, location and builder-track-record content, then on capturing enquiries in a way your sales team can act on once sales open.

faqs.q: Do you work with channel partners and brokers as well as the developer?
faqs.a: We can plan content that supports a partner network, but we work on behalf of the developer or the project team, and the brand voice stays consistent across everything.

faqs.q: How do you reach overseas buyers?
faqs.a: Through video, clear process explainers and campaigns targeted at relevant audiences, with a fast messaging response so distance does not slow the conversation.

faqs.q: Who approves the content before it goes live?
faqs.a: You do. For anything involving approvals, registrations or possession dates, we recommend legal review as part of the approval step.
